clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC5A2, encoding the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT2 that reclaims the bulk of filtered glucose in the early proximal tubule.
Defined by persistent glucosuria with a normal plasma glucose and a normal oral glucose tolerance test, in the absence of any other proximal tubular defect.
Inheritance is co-dominant; homozygous or compound heterozygous individuals show the heaviest urinary glucose loss while heterozygotes may have only mild glucosuria.

Traditionally graded as type A (reduced threshold and reduced maximal reabsorptive capacity), type B (reduced threshold with near-normal maximal capacity) and type O (virtually absent glucose reabsorption).
The great majority of individuals are entirely asymptomatic, the condition being found incidentally on routine urinalysis.
Severe (type O) cases may show polyuria, enuresis, mild volume depletion and a tendency to ketosis during prolonged fasting or pregnancy.
It is a benign isolated transport defect that does not evolve into diabetes mellitus or chronic kidney disease.
Pharmacological SGLT2 inhibition reproduces the same isolated glucosuria, which underscores the essential safety of the inherited condition.
reference.pathophysiology: Filtered glucose is normally reclaimed almost entirely within the proximal tubule, with the high-capacity, low-affinity transporter SGLT2 handling the majority in the early convoluted segment and SGLT1 retrieving the small remainder more distally. Loss-of-function variants in SLC5A2 reduce or abolish SGLT2 activity, lowering the tubular threshold at which glucose begins to spill into the urine and, in the most severe forms, the maximal reabsorptive capacity as well. Glucose therefore appears in the urine despite entirely normal blood concentrations and normal insulin action. Because the lesion is confined to a single apical transporter, the remaining proximal tubular functions - amino-acid, phosphate, urate and bicarbonate handling - stay intact, which distinguishes the disorder from generalised proximal tubulopathy. The obligatory glucose in the tubular fluid can produce a mild osmotic diuresis, and in the type O phenotype the persistent urinary loss of glucose and fluid underlies the occasional dehydration and ketotic tendency seen during fasting or pregnancy.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetes mellitus and impaired glucose tolerance, in which glucosuria accompanies hyperglycaemia
Fanconi syndrome, where glucosuria is joined by generalised aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and bicarbonate wasting
Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (GLUT2/SLC2A2 defect) with hepatorenal glycogen accumulation and disordered glucose homeostasis
Gestational glucosuria from the physiologically lowered threshold of pregnancy
Proximal tubular injury from drugs, heavy metals or paraproteins
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young and neonatal diabetes when hyperglycaemia coexists
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urine glucose alongside a simultaneously drawn plasma glucose
Fasting plasma glucose, glycated haemoglobin and, where needed, an oral glucose tolerance test
Urine amino acids to exclude generalised proximal tubulopathy
Serum phosphate, bicarbonate and urate to confirm that glucose handling is isolated
Renal function and urinary protein to exclude acquired tubular injury
Urinalysis of first-degree relatives given the co-dominant inheritance
redFlags: Coexisting hyperglycaemia or a raised glycated haemoglobin pointing to true diabetes
Aminoaciduria, phosphaturia or acidosis indicating generalised Fanconi syndrome
Hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycaemia and post-prandial hyperglycaemia suggesting Fanconi-Bickel syndrome
Growth failure or rickets, which are not features of isolated renal glucosuria
Symptomatic dehydration or ketosis in a severe (type O) case, particularly during pregnancy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent. Familial renal glucosuria is a benign, non-progressive condition that does not cause diabetes, renal impairment or the metabolic complications of glycaemic disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as diabetes mellitus because the urinalysis was not paired with a plasma glucose measurement.
Failing to exclude generalised Fanconi syndrome, in which glucosuria is only one component of a broader proximal leak.
Confusing it with Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, a glycogen-storage disorder with hepatomegaly and disordered glucose homeostasis rather than an isolated transporter defect.
Attributing coincidental symptoms to the glucosuria when the condition is almost always clinically silent.
Overlooking pregnancy, where the lowered renal threshold can unmask or exaggerate glucosuria.
